title: Ang 96–97: the letters
tomorrow: who could be your father, mother and brother all at once?
last: THE FIFTH GURU · TRUTH, LIVED · THE FOUR WATCHES.

lines: THE TEXT YOU WRITE AND DELETE.
cards: Missing someone has its own grammar: the long text you write and delete, the photo you almost send, the two words you finally do. So what do you write when you miss someone that much?
Tradition says a young Arjan, sent away to Lahore, missed his father, Guru Ram Das, so badly that he wrote to him in verse. Those letters are on ang 96.

teach.h: LIKE THE RAINBIRD CRYING FOR RAIN.
teach.b: The first letter, in paraphrase: my mind longs for the sight of the Guru; it cries out like the rainbird crying for rain. The chatrik, the rainbird of Punjabi poetry, waits for one kind of water only.

teach.h: A MOMENT APART, A DARK AGE.
teach.b: Later, in paraphrase: when I couldn't meet you for a single moment, it was a dark age for me. Tradition tells the rest like a story. The first letters never reached Guru Ram Das; they were held back on the way.
The third got through, and the Guru called his son home. When they met, the last verse is joy, not longing. Sikhs know these hymns as the Shabad Hazare, and some keep them in their daily prayers.
Notice what the week has been doing. A shelter to grip. Truth carried into the hands.
A night that's still yours. A ballad that carries love. Voices from outside the line.
A friend on the road. And now a son who can't stand the distance. A week of pages, and every one of them about closeness.

how: Sikhs know the hymns on ang 96–97 as the Shabad Hazare; some recite them daily, and the story of the young Arjan's letters to Guru Ram Das is told at the gurdwara and at home.

s: tradition says the first letters never reached Guru Ram Das
they were held back on the way; the third got through, and he called his son home.
the letters are short prose notes
they're hymns, in verse, and they stand in the Granth on ang 96.
the chatrik is a bird that drinks from any water
in Punjabi poetry it waits for rain alone; that's the longing.

games.q: your friend moved across the country and keeps sending long messages. you're busy, and you've let three go unanswered. what does ang 96 suggest?
o: wait until you have time for a long reply that matches hers.
longing that reaches out deserves an answer; write back, plainly.
let it fade; distance is part of growing up.
games.why: Arjan's letters are plain longing, and the third one gets through. the story's turn is the answer: the Guru calls him home.

practice: If you can, open ang 96 and read the first letter. Bring to mind someone you miss, near or far, here or gone. Write them a few lines, on paper or in your notes, the way Arjan did: plain, honest, nothing clever.
You don't have to send it. Then sit with the longing itself, without hurrying it along.
